As noted in the Interim Report, we believe that the users and suppliers of transportation services will benefit by the expeditious implementation of a rule upon which they can base their actions. Furthermore, ad hoc considerations of specific commercial zones at individual cities would inevitably result in proceedings that would be overly adjudicatory in nature. This has been a traditional characteristic of individual determinations and would, no doubt, continue to pose a problem.
A goal of this proceeding is to avoid two inherent effects of ad hoc adjudications of commercial zone size - that is, the disparate treatment accorded different cities not due solely to the economic facts peculiar to the local transportation market and the detailed, complicated zone descriptions resulting from individual determinations.

A perusal of the sections contained in 49 CFR 1048 will illustrate the latter problem. A general rule that is clearly stated and easily applied should lead to substantial gains in predictability and public comprehension.
In the Interim Report we considered DOT's proposal that the Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area (SMSA) concept be utilized as the cornerstone of any method used to define collectively commercial zones. The criteria used to define SMSA's - urban population, population growth, population density, proportion of labor force engaged in nonagricultural pursuits, and employment commuting patterns - 35 are certainly relevant to the size of commercial zones.
A complete description of the criteria used to determine SMSA's is contained in Appendix B to the Interim Report, Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 194-198.
